lyocell.origin: Lyocell is regenerated cellulose spun from dissolving wood pulp, like viscose, but the pulp is dissolved directly in an organic solvent instead of being converted to a chemical derivative. The solvent is N-methylmorpholine N-oxide (NMMO) in water. More than one technology line exists: Courtaulds industrialized the process as Tencel, now a Lenzing brand, and the German engineering company Zimmer AG developed its own lyocell process. Research groups use the same solvent to spin fibers from bacterial cellulose, recycled textiles and additive-loaded dopes, which makes lyocell a common platform for functional cellulose fibers.
lyocell.structure: The fiber is cellulose II. Because the chains are dissolved without chemical modification and are stretched in an air gap before they coagulate, they end up highly oriented and crystalline. X-ray microdiffraction of air-gap spun, lyocell-type fibers shows a skin-core structure with microfibrils about 100 nm across, built from ribbon-like elementary fibrils about 6 by 2 nm and stacked more regularly than in viscose, which underlies their higher wet strength. The cross-section is round to oval and smooth. The long, aligned fibrils are weakly bonded sideways, so under wet abrasion they split from the surface: fibrillation, the fiber's defining weakness. Carboxyl content is lower than viscose, about 15 versus 20 mmol/kg in one study.
lyocell.process: Pulp is mixed with aqueous NMMO, and water is evaporated under vacuum until the cellulose dissolves into a viscous dope; plants monitor and model this slurry step closely because the NMMO-to-cellulose ratio and temperature control dissolution. The filtered dope is extruded through spinnerets across a short air gap, where the filaments are drawn while still fluid, into a dilute aqueous NMMO bath in which cellulose precipitates (dry-jet wet spinning). Filaments are washed free of solvent, finished, dried and cut to staple or kept as filament. The solvent is recovered by evaporation and purification; recovery above 99% is reported, and Lenzing states more than 99.8% for its process. Additives such as silver particles or seaweed can be mixed into the dope.
lyocell.performance: Lyocell's moisture regain is roughly 11% at standard conditions, a little below viscose, and it keeps most of its strength wet: one comparison reported about 32 cN/tex dry and 29 wet, where viscose loses close to half. Fabrics are therefore more stable in washing and suit denim, shirting and bedding. It dyes with cellulose dye classes and chars rather than melts. The main problem is fibrillation during wet processing and laundering, which produces a hairy surface and can affect appearance and durability; finishers counter it with cross-linking agents, enzyme treatments and coatings, or exploit it for a soft peach-skin touch.
lyocell.identify: Burn tests are indicative only; lyocell burns like other cellulose, with a paper-like smell and soft ash. Microscopy shows smooth, round to oval, featureless fibers without the serrations of regular viscose, and wet rubbing may raise fine fibrils. FTIR confirms cellulose but not the process. Distinguishing lyocell from modal or cupro can require specialist microscopy or producer documentation, and brand names such as TENCEL cover more than one generic fiber, so the generic name on the label is what identifies it.
lyocell.labeling: 16 CFR 303.7 allows the name lyocell, within the rayon definition, for cellulose precipitated from an organic solution in which no substitution of the hydroxyl groups takes place and no chemical intermediates are formed. The FTC approved the name in 1996 after a petition by Courtaulds. The EU lists lyocell separately under Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011. Producer claims about solvent recovery, pulp sourcing or biodegradability are not part of the fiber name and must be checked against certificates for the specific product.
lyocell.past: Direct dissolution of cellulose in amine oxides offered a route to regenerated fiber without carbon disulfide. Courtaulds brought it to commercial scale under the Tencel name in the early 1990s at Mobile, Alabama, petitioned the FTC in 1992 for a new generic name, and saw lyocell adopted in 1996. Lenzing acquired the Tencel business in 2004. The solvent platform now supports recycling research: in a 2026 study, dope-dyed viscose respun by the NMMO-lyocell route gave fibers of up to about 32 cN/tex with a color shift below Delta E 1, while the viscose route partly depolymerized the cellulose.
facts: above 99% reported; more than 99.8% claimed by Lenzing
